messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi is a 68-year-old Ghanaian American man, a professional dancer who had spent his life trusting his body to move with precision and grace. That trust shattered on a rainy Tuesday evening eighteen months ago, when his sedan was struck broadside by a delivery truck that had run a red light. The impact crushed the driver’s side door and spun the car across three lanes of traffic. Kofi remembers the sound of tearing metal and the smell of gasoline, but beyond that, the memory is a collection of fragments that refuse to assemble into a story. He knows he was trapped in the wreckage for over an hour while firefighters used the Jaws of Life, but when he tries to deliberately recall the sequence of events—how the truck appeared, what he did with his hands on the wheel—the details slip away like smoke. What remains is a jumble of disconnected images: the shattered windshield, a paramedic’s face leaning in, the hydraulic cutter’s whine. He cannot tell a clear account of what happened, even to himself, and this incompleteness has come to feel like a moral failing, as if he should have paid better attention, should have been more prepared. He has begun to believe that he cannot trust himself to do the right thing in any situation, because if he could not even hold onto his own survival, what else might he miss? The body that had been his instrument for decades now feels like a liability, unreliable and foreign; he finds himself startled by his own heartbeat, suspicious of his own reflexes.

The institutional failure that followed deepened this conviction. The police report concluded that the truck driver had been distracted, but the driver’s insurance company spent months disputing liability, and Kofi’s own insurer initially denied his claim for physical therapy. He had come to believe that the systems meant to protect him—the traffic laws, the insurance industry, even the hospital that discharged him with only a sheet of paper and a prescription for painkillers—had all, in their own ways, let him down. There was no reckoning, no acknowledgment that his life had nearly ended. This absence of justice left him feeling that the world was fundamentally indifferent to his safety, and that only constant vigilance could keep him alive.

That vigilance has taken specific, exhausting forms. Kofi now cannot sit or stand in a room unless his back is against a wall, where he can see every entrance and every face. At the dance studio where he has taught for thirty years, he has rearranged his corner of the space so that the mirrors face away from the door, and he positions himself so that no student can approach from behind. When a rehearsal runs long or a student arrives late, his chest tightens and he assumes something terrible has happened—a car crash, a sudden illness, a catastrophe born of unplanned delay. Unexpected sounds, even a dropped water bottle or a door slamming, make him freeze with his hands up, his body braced for impact. He has stopped going out altogether except for work, and he has cut off contact with the friends he used to see at social gatherings, because every invitation felt like a demand to enter an unpredictable world. He also avoids thinking about anything discussed in his therapy sessions, because even the memory of a conversation about the crash feels like opening a wound that has barely closed.

The consequences have been concrete and relational. Kofi’s daughter, who lives in Atlanta, has stopped calling as frequently because every conversation ends with her asking why he will not visit, why he will not let her pick him up for dinner, why he seems to be disappearing. He has lost two long-standing private students who needed evening lessons, because he cannot bring himself to drive after dark. His savings are dwindling, and he has begun to wonder how much longer he can afford to keep the studio. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last week when a car backfired outside his apartment, and he dropped to the floor, covering his head, and stayed there for twenty minutes, unable to move. He is afraid that he is losing his mind, but more than that, he is afraid that he is losing the only life he has left—the life of a dancer who once moved through the world without fear. He hopes that therapy can give him back a story he can tell, and a body he can trust again.
